recipes.name: CLIP is a 'bag of concepts' with weak grammar
recipes.claim: CLIP is a 'bag of concepts' with weak grammar — it does NOT reliably bind which adjective goes with which noun.
recipes.summary: CLIP behaves cross-modally like a bag-of-words: it registers the SET of concepts present but loses structural/syntactic relationships. It cannot reliably tell 'a yellow submarine and a blue bus' from 'a blue submarine and a yellow bus'. With multiple entities, attributes leak onto the wrong object (color/feature bleed). The binding info partly exists in the embedding but is lost in cross-modal alignment — so prompting around it, not relying on it, is the move.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Don't trust adjective-noun proximity in one breath. For multi-entity scenes, either (a) reduce to ONE attributed subject per prompt/region, (b) use BREAK to isolate each subject+attribute into its own chunk to cut color bleed (e.g. 'red-haired knight, green cloak BREAK silver-haired mage, blue robe'), or (c) use regional conditioning / inpainting for hard color separation. Glue compound attributes into single tokens where the model knows them ('redhead', 'blonde', booru 'green_eyes') instead of free-floating 'green ... eyes'.

recipes.name: The hard ceiling is 77 tokens (75 content + start + end)
recipes.claim: The hard ceiling is 77 tokens (75 content + start + end); past it the tail is SILENTLY dropped in raw diffusers, with zero effect on the image.
recipes.summary: CLIP has exactly 77 learned absolute positional-embedding rows, so position 78+ has no representation. Native diffusers slices the token list at 77 and discards the rest — at most a console warning. This is the single most common 'why did my prompt do nothing' failure: everything after ~token 75 was never seen by the model.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Keep each prompt (or each BREAK chunk) at or under 75 CONTENT tokens. Put the load-bearing tokens (subject, the 2-3 attributes that MUST land) in the first ~20 tokens. Count with a CLIP tokenizer before shipping a template; if the studio's character prompts routinely exceed 75 tokens, that overflow is being thrown away in any raw-diffusers path.

recipes.name: Tag-style vs sentence-style is NOT a CLIP fact
recipes.claim: Tag-style vs sentence-style is NOT a CLIP fact — it depends entirely on what the checkpoint was FINE-TUNED on.
recipes.summary: Base SDXL was captioned with natural-language-ish text, so descriptive phrases read best and pure danbooru tags can produce disjointed results. Anime fine-tunes (NovelAI, Illustrious, Pony, most booru-trained SDXL) were trained on comma-separated booru tags, so 'purple_eyes, 1girl, looking_at_viewer' bind sharply and natural sentences underperform. The CLIP encoder is the same in both; the difference is purely the text distribution the UNet learned to expect. So 'always use tags' / 'always use sentences' are both FOLKLORE when stated unconditionally.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Match prompt style to the checkpoint's training data, per-model. For BASE SDXL: short natural-language descriptive phrases (you may sprinkle recognized booru tags like '1girl', 'upper body'). For booru-trained anime fine-tunes: comma-separated underscore tags, ordered by importance, and prefer the model's known tag vocabulary over prose. Document the expected prompt dialect alongside each checkpoint in the studio's model registry so artists don't cross-apply the wrong style.

recipes.name: CLIP/OpenCLIP behave like a bag-of-words cross-modally
recipes.claim: CLIP/OpenCLIP behave like a bag-of-words cross-modally: they cannot reliably bind which adjective goes with which noun, so multi-attribute character prompts leak.
recipes.summary: Lin et al. prove CLIP matches 'orange square + blue triangle' to 'blue square + orange triangle' — the binding info exists unimodally but is lost in cross-modal cosine alignment. For SDXL (CLIP-L + bigG, both bag-of-words encoders), this means 'red scarf, green eyes, blue coat' frequently swaps colors across items. The more attributes you cram per noun, and the more competing nouns, the worse binding gets. Abstract/narrative tokens make it worse by adding ungrounded directions the U-Net must still attend to.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Bind tightly and order adjacency-first: put each attribute immediately before its noun ('crimson scarf, emerald eyes, navy coat'), one or two attributes per noun max. For SDXL specifically, keep distinct subjects few; if two characters need different colors, expect leakage and consider regional prompting / separate generations rather than one dense prompt.

recipes.name: more descriptive words / richer emotional language = better…
recipes.claim: FOLKLORE-DEBUNKED: 'more descriptive words / richer emotional language = better image' and 'keyword spam fills it in' are false for these encoders.
recipes.summary: The community habit of piling on evocative, emotional, and narrative adjectives ('hauntingly beautiful, deeply sorrowful, a soul worn thin') is counterproductive: per the attention-dilution and brittleness evidence, those tokens add ungrounded directions that steal attention from depictable ones and destabilize the embedding (the studio's exact failure). Equally, 'just keep adding keywords' fails because (a) CLIP truncates past 75 and (b) bag-of-words binding degrades as you add competing nouns. The real lever is depictable DENSITY (visible specifics per token), not word count or emotional intensity. Magic-keyword lists ('masterpiece, 8k, trending on artstation') are weak, dataset-specific aesthetic nudges, not semantic content — harmless filler at best, attention-thieves at worst.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]
recipes.design_implication: Audit every prompt by deleting each word and asking 'does removing this change a pixel?' If no, cut it. Replace emotional/quality adjectives with the visible cause of that impression. Cap aesthetic-tag boilerplate to a few proven tokens at the very end where truncation can claim them harmlessly. Measure prompts by visible-attribute count, not length.

recipes.name: There is a PROVEN geometric ceiling
recipes.claim: There is a PROVEN geometric ceiling: no CLIP-style joint embedding can simultaneously do basic description + attribute binding + spatial relations + negation.
recipes.summary: Multiple 2025-26 results (the 'Is CLIP ideal?' line and negation-geometry work) establish that CLIP's single shared embedding space mathematically cannot represent more than ~two of {object identity, attribute binding, spatial relations, negation} at once; negated/affirmative queries collapse to near-identical embeddings. So 'NOT wearing a hat', 'behind the barrel', 'a cube behind a sphere' are encoder-level impossible for CLIP — they are not prompt-skill problems. T5/Qwen LLM encoders handle these far better because they retain syntactic structure, but on SDXL you are hard-capped.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: On SDXL/CLIP: never rely on negation (no 'without', 'no', 'not') — express the positive visible state instead ('bare head', 'closed door'). Don't trust spatial relations in a single CLIP prompt; compose them with layout tools/inpainting/control. Reserve negation and spatial logic for the T5/Qwen pipelines, and even there keep them simple.

recipes.name: A face starves below a hard pixel floor
recipes.claim: A face starves below a hard pixel floor: the VAE 8x downsample destroys facial detail BEFORE diffusion runs, so a 70px face in a full-body frame is already mush at the latent stage.
recipes.summary: Every SD/SDXL/FLUX/Qwen VAE compresses the image 8x per spatial dimension (e.g. 1024px -> 128x128 latent; 512px -> 64x64). A face occupying ~70px of a 1024px-tall full-body shot lands on roughly an 8x9 patch of latent — fewer cells than the face has features. Detail smaller than the 8px-per-cell threshold is gone before the first denoising step; no prompt token can recover information the VAE already discarded. This is an encoder-independent, upstream-of-text bottleneck.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: For a hero whose FACE matters, do not ask one full-body generation to carry it. Either (a) frame to portrait/cowboy-shot so the head occupies >=512px of frame, or (b) generate full-body first, then crop the head region and regenerate/upscale it as its own >=768px pass (inpaint or detailer), then composite. Treat 'face area in pixels' as a budget you spend, not a prompt you write.

recipes.name: Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image) and Qwen3-4B (Z-Image) are…
recipes.claim: Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image) and Qwen3-4B (Z-Image) are INSTRUCTION-tuned LLM encoders — they reward full natural-language description and punish SDXL-style tag soup, the opposite craft from CLIP.
recipes.summary: Qwen-Image uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B as an MLLM condition encoder with a task-specific system prompt and reads the last-layer hidden states; it has effectively no hard token cap at normal prompt sizes (32k+ context). Z-Image uses Qwen3-4B with a ~512-token reference budget and optional system-prompt templates. Both parse syntax and clause structure, so a coherent sentence ('a weathered swordswoman, mid-30s, with a scar across her left brow and tied-back grey-streaked hair, facing the viewer') outperforms comma-separated tags. The face still has to win pixels (Finding 1), but the encoder itself can follow a sentence-level description of the face.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: For Qwen-Image / Z-Image, write the face as a complete, well-ordered SENTENCE up front, not tags: state framing first ('a close-up portrait of...' or 'a full-body shot of, head clearly visible,'), then the specific facial features as a clause. Keep total under ~512 tokens for Z-Image. You CAN use grammar here — but still convert lore to depictable features (Finding 4 applies to all LLM encoders too).

recipes.name: On T5 (FLUX/Chroma), narrative/abstract prose is not 'free…
recipes.claim: On T5 (FLUX/Chroma), narrative/abstract prose is not 'free flavor' — it consumes the conditioning budget and dilutes the depictable tokens, producing generic mush.
recipes.summary: T5-XXL grounds tokens it can map to visual concepts; non-depictable tokens ('worn by grief', 'guarded and steady', the BACKSTORY of why a patch is faded) have no consistent visual referent, so they contribute diffuse, averaged-out attention that pulls the result toward the prior mean. They don't break T5 (it has 512 real, usable positions with no ~20-token collapse), but they crowd out and weaken the concrete visual tokens around them. This is exactly the observed failure: prose-heavy character prompt -> mushy generic result.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Translate every emotional/backstory beat into a DEPICTABLE consequence before it enters a T5 prompt. 'Worn by grief' -> 'hollow cheeks, dark circles under the eyes, downturned mouth'. 'Guarded and steady' -> 'squared shoulders, level gaze, hand resting on sword hilt'. 'Faded patch from an old war' -> 'frayed grey shoulder patch, threadbare edges'. If a clause names no shape, color, posture, texture, or object, cut it.

recipes.name: more detail always = better' and 'longer is always better'…
recipes.claim: FOLKLORE, DEBUNKED: 'more detail always = better' and 'longer is always better' on LLM encoders. Past the limit it truncates; non-depictable narrative still dilutes.
recipes.summary: Two folklore failures. (1) Length: community testing of LLM-encoder T2I reports detailed scenes benefit from 150-300 words but '60+ words don't necessarily improve results' and over-long prompts risk truncation/artifacts — and crucially, anything past max_sequence_length (512 default in both Qwen-Image and Z-Image) is silently dropped from the tail. (2) The studio's own T5 failure ('worn by grief', 'guarded and steady', backstory of a faded patch) generalizes: even a large LLM encoder can READ those tokens, but the DiT can only condition on DEPICTABLE signal. Abstract/emotional/backstory tokens consume budget and pull the conditioning toward a mushy average. The LLM encoder forgives sentence STRUCTURE that CLIP can't; it does NOT magically render non-visual concepts.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]
recipes.design_implication: Convert every non-depictable trait into a visible CUE before it enters the prompt: 'worn by grief' → 'hollow cheeks, red-rimmed eyes, slumped shoulders'; 'guarded' → 'arms crossed, chin lowered, narrowed eyes'; drop the patch's backstory and just say 'sun-faded crimson patch on the left shoulder'. Keep prompts dense with renderable nouns/adjectives, target ~150-250 words max, and never exceed ~480 tokens (512 default). This rule applies to ALL four encoders — it's just most forgiving on Qwen and most brutal on CLIP/T5.

recipes.name: Qwen-Image-Edit uses a DIFFERENT, instruction-shaped system…
recipes.claim: Qwen-Image-Edit uses a DIFFERENT, instruction-shaped system prompt with VISION tokens and a larger 64-token strip — it is built to follow editing INSTRUCTIONS, not just descriptions.
recipes.summary:
The edit pipeline template is: '<|im_start|>system
Describe the key features of the input image (color, shape, size, texture, objects, background), then explain how the user's text instruction should alter or modify the image. Generate a new image that meets the user's requirements while maintaining consistency with the original input where appropriate.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>{}<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
' with prompt_template_encode_start_idx=64. The presence of <|vision_start|>/<|image_pad|>/<|vision_end|> is exactly why a VLM (not T5) was required — the encoder literally sees the source image alongside your instruction.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: For Qwen-Image-Edit, write an IMPERATIVE edit instruction ('change the patched cloak to faded crimson; keep the face and pose identical'), not a fresh scene description. Explicitly name what to preserve — the system prompt is primed to maintain consistency 'where appropriate', so spell out 'where'.

recipes.name: Qwen-Image silently prepends a FIXED system prompt and…
recipes.claim: Qwen-Image silently prepends a FIXED system prompt and strips its first 34 tokens before conditioning — the system prompt steers the LLM's read but never reaches the image.
recipes.summary:
The diffusers pipeline wraps every prompt as: '<|im_start|>system
Describe the image by detailing the color, shape, size, texture, quantity, text, spatial relationships of the objects and background:<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
{}<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
'. prompt_template_encode_start_idx=34 means the first 34 hidden states (the system span) are dropped; only the user-prompt + assistant hidden states condition the DiT. This is why Qwen-Image rewards prompts phrased as concrete visual DESCRIPTION (color/shape/size/texture/quantity/text/spatial) — the system prompt primes the LLM to extract exactly those axes.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Phrase prompts to answer the built-in system question: state color, shape, size, texture, COUNT, any on-image TEXT (in quotes), and spatial relationships explicitly. 'three brass lanterns, left-to-right, smallest in front' beats 'lanterns'. You do not need to (and cannot usefully) inject your own system prompt in standard pipelines — it is overwritten.

recipes.name: CFG SCALE is the dial on negative strength
recipes.claim: CFG SCALE is the dial on negative strength: higher scale = stronger push away from the negative AND further extrapolation past the positive, which is exactly what produces the 'fried' oversaturated / high-contrast look.
recipes.summary: In eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond), w (the CFG scale) multiplies the whole guidance vector, including the push away from the negative. Raising w makes the negative bite harder but also overshoots: the standard deviation of the resulting latent grows roughly linearly with w. Lin et al. 2023 state plainly 'when w is large, the scale of the resulting x_cfg is very big, causing the image over-exposure problem.' Higher std after VAE decode = blown highlights, crushed blacks, neon over-saturation, plastic skin, halos — the colloquial 'deep-fried' SDXL look. So oversaturation is not a prompt-content bug; it is a direct arithmetic consequence of large w inflating latent magnitude.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Do not 'turn up CFG to make the negative work harder.' For SDXL cel/2.5D art keep CFG 4-7 (start ~5-6); CFG 9+ fries the palette. If you need a stronger negative, ADD a precise negative term rather than raising CFG. Diagnose: if outputs look over-saturated/over-contrasty, your first move is LOWER CFG, not editing the prompt.

recipes.name: The fix for high-CFG frying is Rescale-CFG (a.k.a. guidance…
recipes.claim: The fix for high-CFG frying is Rescale-CFG (a.k.a. guidance rescale / dynamic thresholding), not a better negative prompt — it renormalizes the latent's std back down after CFG.
recipes.summary: Lin et al. 2023 compute the per-image std of the pure-conditional prediction (sigma_pos) and the std of the over-inflated CFG prediction (sigma_cfg), then rescale: x_rescaled = x_cfg * (sigma_pos / sigma_cfg), and blend x_final = phi*x_rescaled + (1-phi)*x_cfg. This pulls the latent magnitude back to a sane range so high CFG keeps its prompt adherence WITHOUT the over-exposure. They report w=7.5, phi=0.7 'works great,' with phi in [0.5, 0.75] looking appealing. Saharia et al.'s dynamic thresholding does the analogous clamp for pixel-space; Rescale-CFG is the latent-space version exposed in ComfyUI as the 'RescaleCFG' node and in diffusers as the guidance_rescale argument.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: When you genuinely need high CFG (e.g. pushing a hard style at CFG 8-10), enable RescaleCFG/guidance_rescale ~0.7 instead of accepting blown-out art. This lets you keep negative-prompt strength high while killing the deep-fried palette. It is a sampler/pipeline setting, not a prompt edit — bake it into the studio's SDXL/Chroma generation preset.

recipes.name: A negative prompt is not a 'filter
recipes.claim: A negative prompt is not a 'filter' — it literally replaces the unconditioned branch of the CFG equation, so generation is pushed along the vector AWAY from the negative embedding.
recipes.summary: Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans 2022) jointly trains a conditional and an unconditional (null-token) denoiser. At each sampling step the guided noise prediction is the linear extrapolation eps_guided = eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond). A negative prompt swaps eps_uncond for eps_neg = eps(x, c-), giving eps_guided = eps_cond + w*(eps_cond - eps_neg). Geometrically the model takes the vector from the negative embedding to the positive embedding and walks PAST the positive by factor w. So the negative is not subtracted feature-by-feature; it just redefines the origin the model extrapolates away from. This is why a negative prompt's effect is relative to the positive — adding the same word to BOTH prompts cancels it out, and a negative term only bites when it differs from the positive direction.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Treat the negative as the 'anchor you flee from,' not a blocklist. Only put things in the negative that are genuinely absent from your positive intent (e.g. 'photographic, 3d render, realistic skin' to defend a flat 2.5D JRPG cel look). Never duplicate a concept in both positive and negative — it nets to zero. Keep it short and directional.

recipes.name: long copy-pasted 'cargo' negatives ('deformed, ugly, poorly…
recipes.claim: FOLKLORE: long copy-pasted 'cargo' negatives ('deformed, ugly, poorly drawn, bad anatomy, extra limbs, lowres, jpeg artifacts...') help a GOOD positive. In practice they mostly flatten variety and on modern models can make output WORSE.
recipes.summary: Each negative token spends a slice of the same finite avoidance budget, so a 30-50 item list spreads suppression thin and, worse, broad terms bleed via concept neighborhoods (negating 'moss' also dims 'grass'/'green'; negating 'ugly' dims whole aesthetic regions), collapsing diversity. arXiv:2406.02965 and the SD3.5/SDXL practitioner consensus both report that removing the negative sometimes IMPROVES complex scenes, and that newer models (SDXL, SD3.5, FLUX, Qwen) need far less or no negative than SD1.5 did. The empirical bottom line: negatives are a corrective for a SPECIFIC observed defect, not a quality multiplier on an already-good prompt. The cargo list is a ritual carried over from SD1.5.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Start with an EMPTY negative. Generate, inspect, and add ONE depictable token only for a defect you actually see. Never paste a stock cargo list. If you're on SDXL/Chroma and the positive is strong, 0-5 negative tokens is the ceiling.

recipes.name: A negative should TARGET a specific observed defect, not…
recipes.claim: A negative should TARGET a specific observed defect, not blindly mirror/oppose the positive -- but it must NOT collide with the positive's own content, or mutual cancellation deletes what you wanted.
recipes.summary: The neutralization mechanism (arXiv:2406.02965) means a negative token cancels the matching positive concept. So mirroring the positive is dangerous: if the positive says 'red cloak' and the negative says 'red', you suppress the cloak's color. Good negatives are ORTHOGONAL to the wanted content -- they name failure modes the model tends to add ('blur, watermark, extra fingers, text'), not attributes you asked for. The exception is deliberate disambiguation: to stop an unwanted reading of an ambiguous positive token, name the unwanted sense in the negative (positive 'crane (bird)', negative 'construction crane'). This is the legitimate 'oppose' use -- opposing an unwanted INTERPRETATION, not opposing your own subject.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Build negatives from observed failure modes orthogonal to your subject, never from words that overlap your positive content. Only 'oppose' the positive to kill a specific wrong reading of an ambiguous token (positive 'bat (animal)' -> negative 'baseball bat').

recipes.name: Per-encoder syntax differs
recipes.claim: Per-encoder syntax differs: CLIP negatives are comma-separated concept tokens; T5/Qwen2.5-VL negatives should be a short natural descriptive phrase -- and both obey the same 77/512 limits and front-loading as the positive.
recipes.summary: CLIP (SDXL) is a causal, contrastively-trained encoder with a hard 77-token window and an EOS token that hoards semantics; it parses tag-like comma lists well and weights front tokens more, so a CLIP negative is best written as a short comma list of concept tags ('blur, watermark, text'). T5-XXL (Chroma, FLUX-base) and Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image) are sentence-level encoders with spread-out contextual attention and a 512-token window; they read prose, so a T5 negative reads better as a brief grammatical clause ('blurry low-detail background with visible compression artifacts'). The 77/512 token limits and front-loading apply to the negative field exactly as to the positive -- a bloated negative truncates and dilutes just like a bloated positive (arXiv:2504.01137 on cross-token info flow; HF FLUX docs on T5's 512 vs CLIP's 77).  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: CLIP/SDXL negative = comma-separated concept tags, front-loaded, well under 77 tokens. T5/Chroma & Qwen negative = one short descriptive phrase. Keep the most important avoid-concept first in both.

recipes.name: The giant 50-term 'worst quality, lowres, bad anatomy, bad…
recipes.claim: The giant 50-term 'worst quality, lowres, bad anatomy, bad hands, extra fingers, ...' block is largely FOLKLORE: most terms are inert and the long string actively DILUTES the few that matter.
recipes.summary: Two mechanisms work against the megablock. (1) Attention dilution: CLIP/T5 self-attention is softmax-normalized to sum to 1, so every token added spreads the fixed attention budget thinner — the 3 words that would have steered get drowned by 47 that don't. Research shows that even at zero scaling, a long negative sequence still 'distracts' image-token attention and can reduce quality. (2) A negative prompt cannot summon detail or anatomy the base model never learned; users testing 'bad hands/bad anatomy' negatives found basically zero measurable effect on hand quality — different seeds varied, but not better than empty-negative. The block is cargo-culted from anime-finetune defaults where a FEW quality tags genuinely fire (next finding), then copy-pasted everywhere it doesn't.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Cap negatives at 3-8 SPECIFIC, model-tested tokens, not 50. Build the list by ablation: generate with empty negative, then add ONE term at a time and keep only terms that visibly change the output for YOUR base+seed. Never paste a 50-word block — it is mostly placebo and measurably dilutes the working terms.

recipes.name: Negative TEXTUAL-INVERSION embeddings (EasyNegative,…
recipes.claim: Negative TEXTUAL-INVERSION embeddings (EasyNegative, ng_deepnegative_v1_75t, bad-hands-5, badhandv4, FastNegativeV2) are SD1.5-only — they are dimensionally incompatible with SDXL and do nothing or corrupt on it.
recipes.summary: An SD1.5 TI embedding is a tensor of learned vectors in the 768-dim CLIP-ViT-L space. SDXL has TWO text encoders (CLIP-L 768 + OpenCLIP-bigG 1280, concatenated to 2048) and a native SDXL embedding stores a vector set for BOTH. A 768-only SD1.5 embedding has no 1280-dim half, so it cannot be injected into SDXL's bigG stream — loaders either error on the dimension mismatch or (in lenient UIs) load garbage that injects noise/off-style. Conversion tools only patch 'part of the text encoder' and are unreliable. None of FLUX/Chroma (T5-XXL) or Qwen/Z-Image (Qwen-VL/Qwen3) share CLIP's token-embedding space at all, so these embeddings are categorically inapplicable there.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Never load EasyNegative / ng_deepnegative / bad-hands-5 / badhandv4 / FastNegativeV2 on SDXL, FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image, or Z-Image — they were trained for SD1.5's single 768-dim CLIP and don't transfer. On SDXL use SDXL-NATIVE negative embeddings only (and verify they help via ablation). On FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image there is no CLIP TI slot at all — use plain-text negatives (if CFG-honoring) instead.

recipes.name: Stacking negatives can BACKFIRE and generate the very thing…
recipes.claim: Stacking negatives can BACKFIRE and generate the very thing you negated — the 'Reverse Activation' phenomenon, strongest with early/high-strength negatives.
recipes.summary: ECCV 2024 (arXiv:2406.02965) is the load-bearing empirical study. Negatives work by Deletion-through-Neutralization: the negative branch must first generate the target object at the same location so the subtraction cancels it. This has a DELAYED EFFECT — peak removal for nouns is around step 5, adjectives plateau ~step 10. If a negative is applied too early (steps 1-4) two effects (Inducing + Momentum, ~99.5% step-to-step noise correlation) can lock generative momentum TOWARD the negated object, materializing it instead of removing it. So a heavy, early, high-CFG negative is not 'more safety' — it raises the odds of summoning the artifact.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Treat negatives as scalpels, not insurance. Keep CFG moderate (SDXL ~5-7), keep the negative SHORT, and don't assume 'more negative = safer' — past a point it inverts. If a specific artifact KEEPS appearing despite being negated, that's Reverse Activation: remove that exact term from the negative (or schedule it to start ~step 5+) rather than strengthening it.

recipes.name: The diagnostic: RIGHT KIND of thing, unlucky INSTANCE ->…
recipes.claim: The diagnostic: RIGHT KIND of thing, unlucky INSTANCE -> re-roll the seed. WRONG KIND of thing -> fix the prompt. Re-rolling a prompt miss only hands you N more of the same miss.
recipes.summary: Empirically, similar prompts initialized from the same noise produce visually similar low-level structure (pose, colour gradients, layout); the prompt guides semantic content but the seed anchors the structural scaffold. So if the model is producing the right category of output and the only problem is THIS instance (an awkward hand, an on-spec but unappealing face, a slightly stiff pose, a minor glitch), the conditioning is doing its job — you just landed on a poor z_T, and a different z_T will land elsewhere. But if a requested element is absent or wrong (missing prop, wrong outfit, ignored 'scar over left eye', generic merc when you asked for a specific silhouette, a non-magnetic character), that absence lives in the conditioning, and every z_T denoised under the same instruction reproduces the same absence. Re-rolling explores the distribution the prompt defines; it cannot add a mode the prompt never requested.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Apply the one-question test: 'If I generated 10 more seeds of THIS exact prompt, would the defect plausibly disappear on some of them?' If yes (bad hand, awkward pose, unappealing-but-on-spec face) -> seed problem, batch it. If no — the miss would recur every time (element absent, attribute ignored, wrong style, generic) -> prompt problem, stop generating and rewrite. The 'generic nobody' failure is a NO: every re-roll returns another generic nobody, because nothing in the prompt makes the character specific.

recipes.name: The production loop is
recipes.claim: The production loop is: find a GOOD seed first, then iterate the PROMPT on it. Lock the winning z_T and refine content against a stable scaffold.
recipes.summary: Because a fixed seed preserves low-level structure (pose, layout, colour) across prompt edits while the prompt re-steers semantics, the efficient pipeline inverts naive trial-and-error: you batch-explore to find a z_T whose composition you love, lock it, then do all subsequent content refinement (style adjectives, attribute fixes, expression, costume detail) on that one seed. Each edit moves only what the token controls; the framing you liked stays put. This is also how you build a character SHEET — lock the hero's hero-seed, then vary the prompt for expressions and angles to keep the silhouette consistent. The trap is doing it backwards (rerolling seeds while ALSO editing the prompt), which confounds the two effects and teaches you nothing.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Two-phase always: (1) EXPLORE — batch seeds on a fixed prompt, pick the composition winner, write down its seed. (2) REFINE — lock that seed and change only the prompt, one lever at a time. Never re-roll the seed and edit the prompt in the same step. When you have your hero pose, keep that seed to spin off expression/angle variants on a consistent silhouette.

recipes.name: Ancestral and SDE samplers (Euler a, DPM2 a, DPM++ 2S a,…
recipes.claim: Ancestral and SDE samplers (Euler a, DPM2 a, DPM++ 2S a, DPM++ SDE, DPM++ 2M SDE) inject FRESH random noise every step, so they are markedly less seed-stable and never fully converge; deterministic samplers (DDIM, Euler, Heun, DPM++ 2M, LMS) reproduce exactly from the same seed.
recipes.summary: Ancestral/SDE variants 'add, in each new step, random variables' — re-adding noise after each denoise step. Because there is always new noise to remove, they never converge, and reproduction can fail even with the identical seed and parameters (different sampler implementations/versions diverge). Deterministic samplers follow a fixed ODE trajectory and give 'the exact same image every single time' for a given seed+settings. This is why an operator chasing reproducibility or a stable base image gets burned by Euler a.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: For the production/consistency pipeline (where you re-render, upscale, or seed-sweep and need stability), use a DETERMINISTIC sampler — DDIM, Euler, Heun, DPM++ 2M / 2M Karras. Reserve ancestral/SDE samplers (Euler a, DPM++ SDE) for exploration/variety where you WANT each step to add character. If a seed 'won't reproduce' despite identical settings, check the sampler first — an ancestral/SDE sampler is the usual culprit, not a bad seed.

recipes.name: A fixed seed does NOT deliver character consistency across…
recipes.claim: A fixed seed does NOT deliver character consistency across images. Consistency comes from prompt identity-blocks, reference conditioning (IP-Adapter/ControlNet), or a trained LoRA — NOT from reusing the seed.
recipes.summary: Holding the seed fixed only holds the STARTING noise fixed; the moment you change the prompt (new scene, new pose) the denoising trajectory diverges and the character changes. Same-seed-same-prompt = same image is a tautology, not consistency across DIFFERENT images. Empirically the reliable consistency methods are: (1) a fixed verbatim character description block in every prompt, (2) reference/pose conditioning to separate identity from scene, and (3) a LoRA fine-tuned on 10-20 images of the character (cited at ~85-95% feature retention). The 'lock the seed for a consistent character' tip is folklore — it is the weakest lever of the four.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: For a recurring JRPG character across many shots, do NOT rely on a fixed seed for identity. Build identity from: a frozen character token-block pasted verbatim into every prompt + IP-Adapter/reference image for the face + a trained character LoRA for production volume. Vary the seed freely between shots to get pose/expression variety — identity is held by the LoRA/reference, not the integer. If two shots of the same character look different, fix the reference/LoRA/prompt-block, not the seed.

recipes.name: A good seed does NOT transfer across different models or…
recipes.claim: A good seed does NOT transfer across different models or samplers. The same integer produces a totally different (and not-necessarily-good) image on a different checkpoint or sampler.
recipes.summary: The seed only selects a point in the noise distribution; it carries no meaning by itself. A different model has different learned weights and a different denoising function, so the same starting noise lands somewhere completely different. A different sampler walks a different ODE/SDE trajectory from the same start. The empirical paper found golden seeds had to be re-discovered per architecture (SD 2.0 vs SDXL Turbo). For a studio running SDXL, Chroma/FLUX, Qwen-Image, and Z-Image side by side, a seed tuned on SDXL is meaningless on FLUX.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: When you switch checkpoint (SDXL -> FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image) or sampler, DISCARD the seed — do not copy it expecting the same look. Re-sweep seeds fresh on the new model. Keep a per-model seed note, never a global one. If a shot looked great on SDXL and you must port it to FLUX, port the PROMPT and reference image, not the seed.

recipes.name: Correct CFG range is model-family-specific
recipes.claim: Correct CFG range is model-family-specific; using SDXL-era CFG on a distilled/flow model (FLUX/Chroma) is itself a cause of 'bad' results that gets misread as a seed problem.
recipes.summary: SD1.5/SDXL want real CFG ~6-8 to follow CLIP prompts. FLUX-dev is guidance-distilled and uses a low distilled 'guidance' value (~1-1.5 typical, sometimes called CFG=1 in samplers); pushing real CFG high on it burns the image. Chroma (FLUX-schnell-derived) and Qwen-Image / Z-Image (MMDiT + large text encoders) have their own defaults. A character that looks washed-out or over-cooked may be a CFG/family mismatch, not a seed or prompt failure.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Lock the family-correct guidance FIRST so prompt adherence is honest: SDXL ~6-8, FLUX-dev distilled-guidance ~1-1.5 (real CFG 1), Chroma/Qwen per their model card. Only once guidance is correct can you trust the 'is this a prompt miss or seed miss' diagnosis -- otherwise a guidance bug masquerades as both.

recipes.name: The seed only chooses the starting Gaussian noise latent
recipes.claim: The seed only chooses the starting Gaussian noise latent; it carries no semantic content of its own.
recipes.summary: Generation begins from a pure-noise latent z_T sampled deterministically from the seed. The denoising network then walks z_T -> z_0 conditioned on the prompt (DDPM reverse process, Ho 2020; latent-space version Rombach 2022). The seed is just the random-number-generator state that fixes z_T byte-for-byte. It does NOT encode 'a slouching man' or any concept -- it is a fixed cloud of static that the model interprets THROUGH the prompt. Same seed + same prompt + same sampler/steps/CFG = pixel-identical image (full determinism); change any one and the trajectory diverges.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Treat the seed as a coordinate, not a content knob. If the IMAGE CONTENT is wrong (generic character, wrong attributes, wrong vibe), the seed is not the lever -- rewrite the prompt. Only re-roll the seed when the content is right but you want a different SAMPLE (different pose/face/framing) of that same described thing.

recipes.name: A weak/underspecified prompt produces a generic…
recipes.claim: A weak/underspecified prompt produces a generic regression-to-the-mean image NO MATTER the seed -- this is the operator's exact failure mode.
recipes.summary: When the prompt under-constrains identity, the model fills the unconstrained degrees of freedom with the dataset average: a neutral, forgettable 'default person' in a default pose. Re-rolling the seed only re-samples WITHIN that generic basin -- you get a different generic nobody every time, never a striking character, because nothing in the conditioning pushes toward specificity. Community guidance is blunt: 'a castle' yields a generic fortress; adding specific descriptors slashes output randomness dramatically because the prompt now constrains the manifold.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: If 2-3 seed re-rolls all give different-but-equally-generic results, STOP re-rolling -- it is a prompt miss. The signature of a prompt miss is 'varied yet uniformly bland.' Add load-bearing identity tokens: distinct silhouette, specific clothing/material, age, explicit pose verb ('standing tall, weight forward'), and an emotional/character descriptor. Then re-roll. Do NOT touch tonemaps/lighting/render settings to fix a content problem.

recipes.name: Encoder type dictates token-ORDER sensitivity
recipes.claim: Encoder type dictates token-ORDER sensitivity: CLIP is strongly order/position sensitive (front-load); T5 and LLM encoders are bidirectional/context-aware (write coherent sentences, bind attributes explicitly).
recipes.summary: CLIP has learned absolute position embeddings and an early-token attention bias, so order matters a lot — first tokens dominate. T5 uses bidirectional full-visibility attention (every token attends to every other), making it far less order-sensitive and good at attribute binding through grammar. Qwen2.5-VL / Qwen3 are causal LLMs that read the prompt as instruction-following language with a prepended system prompt — they reward clear, well-structured natural language and explicit spatial/relational phrasing over keyword soup.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Match structure to encoder. CLIP/SDXL: comma-separated, subject-first, highest priority earliest. T5/FLUX/Chroma: full grammatical sentences with explicit attribute binding ('the knight's tabard is faded green' so 'faded green' binds to 'tabard', not the sky) and explicit spatial language ('centered, three-quarter view'). Qwen-Image/Z-Image (LLM): natural descriptive paragraphs, optionally LLM-expanded; spell out layout, materials, and any rendered text verbatim in quotes. Don't paste the SAME prompt across encoder families.

recipes.name: Negative prompts are a CFG mechanic, not a 'forbidden…
recipes.claim: Negative prompts are a CFG mechanic, not a 'forbidden words' list — and they DON'T exist on guidance-distilled models (FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo).
recipes.summary: CFG runs the model twice — a conditioned (positive) pass and an unconditioned pass — and pushes the result away from the unconditioned prediction: eps = eps(neg) + scale*(eps(pos) - eps(neg)). A negative prompt simply REPLACES the empty unconditioned branch with a second real encode, steering away from it. This requires two passes. FLUX-dev/schnell use *guidance distillation* (guidance baked into a single pass) so they have no genuine unconditioned branch and ignore negative prompts. Z-Image-Turbo is distilled and uses NO CFG at all. Chroma is de-distilled and RE-ENABLES true CFG, so its negative prompt is real (and uses the same T5 cap).  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Maintain negative prompts ONLY for SDXL and Chroma (true-CFG models). For FLUX-dev/schnell and Z-Image-Turbo, delete the negative prompt entirely — it does nothing; bake exclusions into the positive prompt instead ('clean background' rather than negative 'cluttered'). On SDXL, keep negatives a short tag list of genuine failure modes (extra fingers, lowres, jpeg artifacts), not a wishlist — every neg token is a real second encode that steers the unconditioned branch.

recipes.name: There is a length sweet spot, and it is encoder-specific
recipes.claim: There is a length sweet spot, and it is encoder-specific — short for CLIP, medium-detailed for T5, long for LLM encoders; past the sweet spot you get dilution, not detail.
recipes.summary: Adding tokens raises the risk that the mean of the conditioning drifts toward generic and that attributes cross-bind. For CLIP the sweet spot is tiny (~20 effective tokens, community consensus 25-35 anime tags max before confusion). For T5/FLUX, mid-length explicit sentences win; piling on prose dilutes (the studio failure). For Qwen-Image/Z-Image, the official guidance is genuinely long detailed natural-language prompts — these LLM encoders are the ONE place where verbosity helps, because the model parses structure rather than averaging tokens.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Calibrate length to the encoder, don't max it out. SDXL: aim ~25-40 tokens of pure visual content, never pad to 75. FLUX/Chroma: 1-4 tight sentences of depictable facts (well under 256/512). Qwen-Image/Z-Image: write a full detailed paragraph (these reward it) — and ONLY here consider LLM-expanding a short prompt. If a JRPG character result is 'mushy/generic,' the fix is usually FEWER, more concrete tokens, not more.

recipes.name: T5-based diffusion models do NOT respond to non-depictable…
recipes.claim: T5-based diffusion models do NOT respond to non-depictable tokens — emotion/backstory/motive words ('worn by grief', 'guarded and steady', 'why the patch is faded') are dead weight that dilute the visual tokens. THIS IS THE FAILURE.
recipes.summary: Wang et al. (CVPR 2025) show empirically that although T5 was trained on lots of non-visual text in C4, diffusion models with a T5 encoder 'do not respond to those non-visual prompts' — non-visual prompts yield low CLIP-alignment images. The encoder's language capacity is largely redundant for image synthesis (they distill T5-XXL to T5-Base at 1/50th size with comparable image quality). Abstract/emotional concepts have no stable visual referent, so those tokens don't ground; they occupy sequence positions and pull attention mass away from the depictable tokens, producing the 'mushy generic' result you saw.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Translate every non-depictable trait into its VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE before it enters a T5 prompt. Not 'worn by grief, guarded and steady' → instead 'hollow under-eye shadows, downturned mouth, shoulders squared, jaw set, eyes fixed forward.' Not 'a patch faded from years of wear' → 'a sun-bleached cloth shoulder patch with frayed edges.' Delete pure backstory/motive words entirely; they cost tokens and ground nothing.

recipes.name: T5 truncation is SILENT
recipes.claim: T5 truncation is SILENT — past the token limit the tail of the prompt is dropped with no warning, so anything you put last can vanish.
recipes.summary: T5TokenizerFast truncates at max_sequence_length with no error raised to the user. Unlike ComfyUI's CLIP path (which chunks the 77-token stream into concatenated 75-token blocks), the diffusers T5 path does NOT chunk — it hard-truncates. A prompt that over-runs 512/256 simply loses its ending tokens.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Front-load the load-bearing visual tokens (subject, pose, key attributes, palette) in the first ~60% of the prompt. Never bury the character's defining features at the end of a long prompt — put style/lighting boilerplate last where it's safe to lose.
